name: excess-vocabulary
description: Words whose frequency in 2024 PubMed abstracts exceeded the frequency expected from the 2021-2022 trend, as identified and annotated as style words by Kobak et al. The list nominates words for the wording_check; it does not show that a sentence was written or revised by a language model.

source.citation: Kobak D, Gonzalez-Marquez R, Horvat E-A, Lause J. Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary. Science Advances. 2025;11(27):eadt3813.
source.data: https://github.com/berenslab/llm-excess-vocab (results/excess_words.csv and results/yearly-counts.csv.gz, MIT License, Copyright (c) 2024 Dmitry Kobak, Rita Gonzalez-Marquez)

selection: From the authors' annotated list of 900 excess words (2013-2024), the words annotated as style words (type style, style/content, or style/count) were kept when their 2024 frequency exceeded a linear extrapolation of the 2021 and 2022 frequencies by a gap above 0.01 or a ratio above 1.5, computed from the authors' yearly-counts matrix. This gives 366 words; the paper reports 379 excess style words for 2024 under its own thresholds, so the two sets differ at the margin. Word forms are the authors' (inflections are separate entries); matching is on the lower-cased exact form.
limits: The paper estimates a lower bound: an abstract revised by a language model that uses none of these words is not counted, so a passage without them is not shown to be free of such revision.
The paper cannot separate direct language-model use from authors who adopted the vocabulary themselves; a count says nothing about who wrote the sentence or how.
Preprints on 2024-2025 text report that authors avoid words once they are named, so the list ages: a low count in a recent manuscript is weaker evidence than it was for 2024 text.
A count nominates a passage for the editor's wording_check in context. It is not a finding, not a measure of reading difficulty, and never a judgment that a text is machine-written.
